body.p: Reconsideration of this Application and entry of the Amendment are respectfully requested. Claims 1-21 are pending in the application, with claims 1, 9, 19 and 20 being the independent claims. Claims 1, 4, 9, 16, 19, and 20 are amended. Claim 21 is new. Support for the amendments may be found throughout the as-filed specification. No new matter has been added.

Claim 16 is objected to for allegedly being presented in a contingency format. OA, p. 2. Without acquiescing to the propriety of the objection, and solely in an effort to advance prosecution, claim 16 has been amended to address this objection. 35 U.S.C. 4101 Claim Re jections
Claims 9, 18, and 20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. @ 101 for allegedly being directed to an abstract idea without significantly more. OA, p. 2-4. Applicant respectfully traverses this rej ecti on.
Step 2A

The Supreme Court has held that "[a]t some level, all inventions embody, use, reflect, rest upon, or apply laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas," and has cautioned "to tread carefully in construing this exclusionary principle lest it swallow all of patent law." Alice Corp., 573 U.S. at 216, 110 USPQ2d at 1980 (citing Mayo, 566 US at 71, 101 USPQ2d at 1965). An invention is not ineligible simply because it involves an abstract concept. Rather, the claim as a whole must be directed to an abstract idea.

With regard to independent claims 9 and 20, the OA alleges that "other than reciting a 'processing circuit', nothing in the claim element precludes the step from practically being performed in the mind." OA, p. 3. The OA then further states that "if a claim limitation, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, covers performance of the limitation in the mind but for the recitation of generic computer components, then it falls within the 'Mental Process' grouping of abstract ideas". OA, p. 3-4. This is incorrect.
The MPEP provides, at @2106.04(II), that Step 2A determines whether the claim as a whole is not directed to a judicial exception and thus is eligible. The MPEP further provides, at

§2106.03, that software expressed as code or a set of instructions detached from any medium is an idea without physical embodiment. This is clearly not the case for independent claims 9 and 20. For example, both independent claims 9 and 20 recite similar features directed to: a control system configured to communicate with a robot having a robot arm that includes or is attached to an end effector apparatus, and having a camera attached to the robot arm; at least one processing circuit configured, when the robot is in a loading environment...and a queue of objects. The invention of independent claims 9 and 20 includes a control system configured for communication with a tangible robot, and a processing circuit configured to perform steps related to tangible objects, i.e., a queue of objects.

The MPEP also provides, at §2106.04(a)(2) III A that "[a] claim with limitation(s) that cannot practically be performed in the human mind does not recite a mental process." See SRI Int'l, Inc. v. Cisco Systems, Inc., 930 F.3d 1295, 1304 (Fed. Cir. 2019). The steps of processing loading environment image information received from a camera, identifying a loading environment state from the image information, executing a pallet detection operation after a pallet swap operation, detecting an existing pallet in the loading environment from the image information, determining a pallet fill status, identifying a pallet identifier, and determining an object movement command based on a comparison of existing object type identifiers, incoming object type identifiers, and a pallet identifier, recited in independent claims 9 and 20, are described in greater detail at paragraphs [0111]-[0120]. These features may require steps such as computational analysis of digital images, using, for example, spatial structure information, depth information, point clouds, etc. Such manipulation and analysis of digital image information cannot practically be performed in the human mind or on paper, as the OA asserts. These aspects of the claims is similar to those in Research Corp. Techs., 627 F.3d at 868, 97 USPQ2d at 1280, where the claims required the manipulation of digital image data and the output of a specific computer data structure. See MPEP §2106.04(a)(2) III A. The claims in Research Corp Techs. were found to be directed to patent eligible subject matter. Just as the claims in Research Corp Techs. were not found to recite a mental process because they require the computational analysis of digital image data structures and generation of new computer data structures based thereon, the present claims also do not recite a mental process.
Even if the claims are determined to recite an abstract idea under prong 1, which Applicant does not concede, the claims remain patent eligible because, under Step 2A, prong 2, the claims

are not directed to this alleged abstract idea because any abstract idea is integrated into a practical solution that addresses a technical problem arising in the relevant technical field. Independent claims 9 and 20, as amended, are directed to a technical solution which solves a problem specifically arising in the technical field of robotic systems. The invention as recited by independent claims 9 and 20 provide technical improvements to a robotic system configured for use in a loading environment. See Specification, para. [0031]. These technical improvements increase the speed and precision of planning for and executing the retrieval and placement of objects within a loading environment. It further provides the technical improvement to the efficiency of palletization or de-palletization operations conducted within and adjacent to the loading environment. Id.

Specifically, the claims address this technical problem by processing loading environment image information received from a camera. As described, for example, at paragraph [0039], the image information describes or otherwise represents an environment in which the camera is located The image information may represent objects located on premises (such as a warehouse, a manufacturing plant, a retail space, etc.), such as boxes, bins, cases, crates, pallets, or other containers. This image information is processed to distinguish between individual objects in the camera field of view to perform object recognition and object registration based on the image information, and to perform robot interaction planning based on the image information.

In contrast to the existing technology in the field, where robots often lack the sophistication necessary to duplicate human interactions required for executing larger and/or more complex tasks such as processing image information to distinguish between individual objects in a field of view to perform robot interaction planning, the present inventive technology can process loading environment image to identify a loading environment state, execute a pallet detection operation after a pallet swap operation, detect an existing pallet, determine the pallets fill status, identify the pallet, and determine object movement commands based on comparisons between multiple types of identifiers, thus providing an improved efficiency of palletization or de-palletization operations conducted within and adjacent to loading environments. See Specification, paras. [0031]-[0033].

In the Office's Revised Guidance for Determining Subject Matter Eligibility dated February 7, 2019 (hereinafter "Bahr Memo")', Step 2A (Prong Two) requires an evaluation of additional elements "to determine whether they integrate the exception into a practical application of the exception." See Bahr Memo, p. 13. The MPEP further provides that "a claim reciting a judicial exception is not directed to the judicial exception if it also recites additional elements demonstrating that the claim as a whole [emphasis added] integrates the exception into a practical application. One way to demonstrate such integration is when the claimed invention improves the functioning of a computer or improves another technology or technical field [emphasis added]." MPEP § 2106.04(d)(1).
As previously described above, the Specification describes the above-noted improvement to the technological field of computing systems and methods for processing spatial structure data:

The technology described herein provides technical improvements to a robotic system configured for use in a loading environment. Technical improvements described herein increase the speed and precision of planning for and executing the retrieval and placement of objects within a loading environment. The robotic system further provides improvements to the efficiency of palletization or de- palletization operations conducted within and adjacent to the loading environment.

Specification, para. [0031]. These improvements to the field are reflected in the computing system of independent claim 9, and the robotic control method of claim 20, as amended. The Patent Trial and Appeal Board has previously looked to problem-solution statements in relevant specifications to determine that claims were patent-eligible, as in the case of Ex Parte Plondke2, for example.

The practical application of the present claims is similar to that found in the Research Corp. Techs. case, discussed above. Similar to that case, the present claims are directed to the computer based analysis of a digital image, requiring the manipulation of computer data structures and the output of newly generated computer data structures with a practical application. See MPEP §2106.04(a)(2) III A. There are also significant parallels between the present case and McRO, Inc.
i Accessible at:

2 PTAB looked to the specification and determined the claims were directed to providing "faster search times", which solve "the art recognized problem of determining a global extremum without consuming 'intensive' computing resources", and thus were not directed to an abstract idea. Ex Parte Plondke, Appeal No. 2016-006905 (PTAB 2017).

v. Bandai Namco Games Am. Inc.. 837 F.3d 1299, 120 USPQ2d 1091 (Fed. Cir. 2016). Just as in McRO, the present claims recite specific computer functionality, described in specific detail in the specification, to permit a computer system to perform a task that could previously only be performed with subject intervention by a human. In McRO, this task related to specific animation tasks. In the present case, the task relates to identifying a loading environment state, detecting a pallet and its fill status, then determining an object movement command by comparing multiple types of identifiers. Accordingly, just as in Research Corp. Techs. and McRO, the present claims are patent eligible.

Thus, under Step 2A, prong 2, independent claims 9 and 20, and claim 18 indirectly dependent upon claim 9, are not directed to an abstract idea because any abstract ideas recited therein are integrated into a practical application that improves the technological field of computing systems and methods for determining and facilitating the picking and placement of objects in an environment around a robot.
Step 2B

Even if the claims are found to be directed to an abstract idea under Step 2A in light of the above arguments - a conclusion that is not being conceded herein - the claims nonetheless recite additional elements which amount to significantly more than the judicial exception. The Bahr memo states that "Revised Step 2A overlaps with Step 2B, and thus, many of the considerations need not be reevaluated in Step 2B because the answer will be the same." See Bahr Memo, p. 19. Examples of features that indicate an inventive concept include "improvements.. .to any other technology or technical field", such as the improvements of the present invention previously discussed above. As discussed above, the invention as recited by claims 9, 18, and 20 provides an unconventional improvement to computing systems and methods for determining and facilitating the picking and placement of objects in an environment around a robot.

The Offices alleges that, with regard to independent claims 9 and 20: "[t]he claim does not include additional elements that are sufficient to amount to significantly more than the judicial exception." OA, p. 4. However, the Bahr Memo provides examples of features that indicate an inventive concept, including "improvements to the functioning...to any other technology or technical field;" or "applying the judicial exception with, or by use of, a particular machine." Bahr Memo, p. 20.

Amended independent claims 9 and 20 provide more than just "mere instructions to apply the exception using a generic computer component" as suggested on p. 4 of the OA. For example, the features including: processing loading environment image information received from the camera; identifying a loading environment state from the processed loading environment image information, the loading environment state including a plurality of existing object type identifiers respectively associated with the existing objects and a plurality of incoming object type identifiers associated with respective incoming objects; executing a pallet detection operation after a pallet swap operation to: detect an existing pallet in the loading environment from the loading environment image information, determine a pallet fill status of the existing pallet, and identify a pallet identifier associated with the existing pallet; and determining an object moving command to be performed based on a comparison between the plurality of existing object type identifiers, the plurality of incoming object type identifiers, and the pallet identifier, as recited in independent claim 9 (and similarly recited in independent claim 20) are significantly more than an abstract idea, as the computer systems and methods of independent claims 9 and 20 are capable of performing the above-mentioned steps to achieve an improved efficiency of palletization or de-palletization operations conducted by a robot within and adjacent to loading environments. See Specification, paragraphs [0111]-[0120], for example. This is unlike prior systems which lack the sophistication necessary to duplicate such a complex task. Amended claims 9 and 20 therefore provide an inventive concept in the form of improvements to a technology or technological field.

Therefore, it is respectfully submitted that even if the Office finds the invention as recited in claims 9, 18, and 20 to be directed to an abstract idea under Step 2A (a conclusion which Applicant does not concede to herein), the invention nonetheless amounts to significantly more under Step 2B, and must be deemed patent-eligible. Thus, it is respectfully requested that the outstanding rejection under 35 U.S.C. §101 be withdrawn. 35 U.S.C. X103 Claim Rejections

Claims 1-20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being anticipated by JP 2020- 196612 to Diankov, et al. ("Diankov") in view of U.S. Publ. No. 2018/036159 to Paquin, et al. ("Paquin"). OA, p. 5-17.
Independent claim 1 is amended to recite "executing a pallet detection operation after a pallet swap operation to determine a pallet fill status of a pallet at the loading environment."
Independent claims 9, 19, and 20 are amended to recite similar features. Thus, the arguments presented below are applicable mutatis mutandis to independent claims 1, 9, 19, and 20.

With regard to independent claims 9 and 20, the feature of "executing a pallet detection operation" was alleged to be disclosed by Diankov on p. 9 of the OA. Diankov, however, does not disclose the above-cited features of amended independent claims 1, 9, 19, and 20. For example, the cited paragraph [0035] and claim 2 of Diankov only discloses generating representations of a detected environment and is silent with respect to pallet detection or pallet swaps. Further, with respect to claim 16 of the present application, the Office cites [0145] of Diankov as purportedly disclosing a pallet swap command. This is incorrect. The cited portion of Diankov is directed to the detection of packages within a storage area and is unrelated to pallets or pallet swapping. Diankov does not disclose executing a pallet detection operation after a pallet swap operation. Diankov is silent with respect to any disclosure pertaining to swapping/replacing a pallet. Similarly, Paquin does not disclose any such features.

The combination of Diankov and Paquin therefore do not teach or suggest at least the above-cited features of independent claims 1, 9, 19, and 20. Thus, independent claims 1, 9, 19, and 20 are patentable. Claims 2-8, 10-18, and new claim 21 depend from and add further features to independent claims 1 and 9, and are thus patentable for the same reasons.
It is therefore respectfully requested that the outstanding rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 103 be withdrawn.
